note: Compatibility corpus: the bash snippets an agent actually writes, each with the POSIX-correct expectation. `severity: must-match` means the output is asserted exactly as Linux bash would produce it; `severity: platform-difference` has no expectation because the Windows shape is recorded into the baseline instead (read-only facts such as `uname` or the `ls -l` permission column). `needs` names the external commands a case depends on: a missing one is a SKIP, which is how a partially installed toolchain still produces a meaningful score. `host: true` means the need comes from the host OS rather than this project's toolchain, so FULL mode tolerates its absence. A case whose exit status is 0 while its output is wrong is counted as `silent-wrong`, which no baseline may contain.

cases.note: The drive-mount rewrite reads text, not intent, so `/<letter>/…` in a program's *script* operand is rewritten with it and the program fails loudly (`sed '/x/d'` sees `X:\d`). Recorded rather than asserted: the wording is the tool's own, and the escape hatch is the next case. The contract states this boundary so a model writes `sed '/x/d'` with `DSH_BASH_NATIVE_NO_PATHCONV=1` (or an equivalent expression) instead of debugging it.

cases.note: The same boundary seen from awk, where the operand that gets rewritten is the program itself (`awk '/x/{print}'` fails on `X:\{print}`). The contract names this shape and the rewrite that avoids it (`awk '$0 ~ /x/'`).

cases.note: The program form of `rm` reaches a child process through the plugin's shim directory (patch 0016), whose path is per-engine and therefore not composable from here: `test-package.mjs` gates that the shim name is the engine itself and that this same command refuses. cases.note: `-ef` is `stat` on Unix: two paths name one file when they resolve to the same (device, inode). This engine answered `not supported on this platform` to every form of it until patch 0020 gave it the Windows pair — the volume serial number and the file index — so the three cases here and beside it are the rule rather than an edge of it.
Two files that exist and differ answer false; a path-string comparison would also get this right, which is why it is `test-ef-same-file` and `test-ef-directory` that carry the weight.
bash answers false for an operand that is not there rather than reporting an error, which is what a missing file has to keep doing once the identity query exists.
A directory is the case that needs `FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS` on the handle, and `./d` is a second spelling of the same directory rather than the same string.
